q: Why have geneticists paused their own research four times in history?
a:
Geneticists paused their own research four times because each time a new technology emerged, they became frightened enough by the possible risks that they chose to stop until safety could be better assessed.

- Cobb frames this as unique in the history of science — no other field, not even the scientists building the atomic bomb, has voluntarily halted its own work over safety fears [7:58].
- The first two moratoriums came in 1972 and 1975, centered on a famous meeting on the California coast about "recombinant DNA," where roughly 200 scientists discussed how to do the experiments safely without risking things like unintended pandemics [9:54].
- The discussion was entirely about safety, not whether the work should be done at all, and it was self-regulated by scientists themselves rather than involving the public [10:26].
- More broadly, Cobb describes it as geneticists becoming "so frightened and so alarmed by what they've done" that they imposed a pause — sometimes lasting months — until they felt sure the work could proceed safely [7:29].
- He notes there are three newer developments he sees as raising similar alarm today, echoing the same pattern of fear followed by resolution seen in the earlier pauses [8:23].
